title: Stewards decision on McLaren Singapore Sprint clash revealed
excerpt:
Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have both escaped punishment after the McLaren team mates collided on the final lap of the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint.

The incident took place at Turn 5 as the duo chased Charles Leclerc's Ferrari for the final step on the podium, with Norris diving to the inside of his team mate ahead, which resulted in the pair making contact and spinning.

While Piastri retired after hitting the wall, Norris recovered and was able to reach the chequered flag in P8.

Post-Sprint, the stewards investigated the incident and decided that no further action would be taken.

"The driver of Car 81 explained that he had not expected Car 1 to attempt an overtake and, after turning in, noticed Car 1 on the inside and attempted to leave space," noted the stewards' report.

"The driver of Car 1 said that he saw an opportunity to overtake. He said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of Car 81 prior to the apex and therefore expected to be left space. As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated so he had to use the inside kerb and braked and a collision occurred."

The stewards concluded that, "both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision. Therefore the Stewards determined to take no further action."

On the incident and before the stewards' investigation, Norris stated: "I think the pace was very strong. Obviously we were just stuck the whole race, and the last lap there was a big opportunity into Turn 5.

"I went for it, the gap closed bit more than I would have liked. Obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing, so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one.

"It was a big gap, I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri said: "I need to look at it. I didn't see him at the apex.

"I looked behind into the corner and saw he was a reasonable way behind for a corner like that but I'll have a look and the team can do what it needs to do."

title: Perez and Stroll reflect on Singapore Sprint clash
excerpt:
Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll have shared their reactions after a collision during the early stages of the Singapore Sprint forced both to retire.

Following a delayed start to proceedings due to heavy rainfall, the 100km dash got underway in challenging conditions – and just as George Russell crashed out of the lead at the front towards the end of the first lap, Stroll had also pulled off track further down the field.

Replays showed that the Aston Martin driver had clashed with the Cadillac of Perez at Turn 16, putting Stroll immediately out of the event. Perez, meanwhile, limped back to the pits but also went on to retire due to the damage sustained on his car.

It was confirmed that the incident would be investigated after the Sprint but the stewards ultimately decided that no further action needed to be taken, their view being that “the driver of Car 18 [Stroll] took a reasonable line into the corner and therefore was not at fault”.

Prior to the outcome of the investigation being announced, Perez gave his take on what happened and admitted that he was left to wonder what could have been given the weather conditions.

“It was a big shame because it was a bit of an opportunity, although the race is pretty short,” the Mexican explained. “I hope we get these conditions later on in the weekend.

“I was on the inside into Turn 16 with Lance and I wasn’t expecting him to shut the door there. When he closed the door I tried to brake, but it was just too late. I ended up locking, and there was nothing I could have done.”

Stroll, meanwhile, conceded that he had not yet had time to review the incident, commenting: “I don’t know exactly what happened. I got hit.”

Pushed on how difficult the conditions had been to drive in, the Canadian added: “Not so hard, I just got hit.”

title: Hamilton delighted with ‘mega start’ in Singapore Sprint
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was thrilled by the opportunity to showcase his skills in wet conditions during the Singapore Sprint, with the Ferrari driver charging from P6 to the podium positions on the opening lap.

After feeling frustrated by his lack of pace on soft tyres in Sprint Qualifying, Hamilton executed a superb launch that saw him overtake both McLarens as well as his team mate Charles Leclerc on the damp track.

When George Russell crashed out of the Sprint, he gained another place and cleverly managed the remaining laps to secure P2, crossing the line 2.5s behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.

“I had a mega start which is awesome,” he reflected. “I love driving this track in the rain and those conditions, so as soon as the heavens opened I was like, ‘This is a great day’.

“I was trying to get close to [Verstappen] without killing my tyres, so I wasn't really pushing that much but I was bringing him in. Then I just realised that, at this point, we've still got a long way to go, I don't think we'll be able to overtake in these conditions, there's only one line, and so I backed off and then the right side started to overheat a little bit.

“But then I got the control back, sorted, and then towards the end I started to push and started to close the gap, but it's a tough track to overtake.”

The performance gave Hamilton confidence that Ferrari can put it all together in Qualifying and take the fight to their rivals, with the Briton targeting a fifth victory at the Marina Bay Circuit to equal Sebastian Vettel’s record.

He said: “I think we showed that we obviously have a good car. I think if we can do slightly better in Qualifying, get both cars up there, I think we'll be able to reapply pressure tomorrow to both the Mercedes and the Red Bull.

“They are quick, of course, but we can be there hounding them, so hopefully we can position the car in a slightly better position in this Qualifying session coming up.”

Leclerc was slightly less enthused by his P3 finish in the Sprint due to relentless issues with his intermediate tyres. At one stage, he instructed his engineer to “leave me alone” when asked to cool the rubber along the straights, before complaining about degradation.

“I struggled a lot from mid-race onwards,” Leclerc explained. “I went towards a quite aggressive balance on the other side of what I normally do with quite a weak front, which was quite good for the first half of the race, but then when it dried up I was nowhere, so it was kind of tricky at the end.”

He was nevertheless able to hold off Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in a late battle for the final spot on the podium, which came to an end when the McLaren pair collided on the last lap.

Reflecting on the incident, he added: “I knew I had to have a very good exit out of [Turn] 5 because I was very weak in all right-hand corners, particularly with the front left.

“I had quite a good exit but then I checked in my mirrors and I saw red lights on the back of the cars of the McLarens, so I knew that something happened. Kimi [Antonelli] was also very strong towards the end so, yeah, we just didn't have the pace at the end.”

title: Verstappen admits concern over ‘horrendous’ Sprint start
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was delighted to secure his first Singapore win after taking victory in the Sprint, but the Dutchman cautioned that Red Bull need to improve on their starts following an “horrendous” launch.

After a delay to the event beginning due to heavy rain, Verstappen had a slow getaway from pole position when the action did get underway – resulting in Mercedes’ George Russell snatching the lead.

The picture soon changed, however, when Russell spun out off the final corner at the end of the first tour and crashed out of the Sprint, putting Verstappen back into P1.

From there the four-time World Champion handled the tricky conditions and kept a chasing Lewis Hamilton at bay to claim victory, his first at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Despite being pleased with his triumph, Verstappen conceded after the event that the launch would be a key area to focus on given the impact that a poor getaway could have on Sunday.

“The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on, because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over if nothing crazy happens,” the 29-year-old explained.

“So, yeah, not ideal, but then we got a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner. And after that, we just wanted to keep it calm and under control, because you know that you can't pass around here, and especially in a condition like this with the intermediates.

“We just tried to bring it home, and of course, happy to win here in the Sprint, but I also know that I want to win tomorrow.”

Pushed on how it felt to finally win in Singapore – with it previously being the only circuit on the current calendar that Verstappen had not triumphed at – the Red Bull driver reiterated that his focus remained on doing so again in the Grand Prix.

“I want to win tomorrow,” he responded. “I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix. We need to have a good Qualifying.

“It will be very close with a lot of cars I think, and we just need to try to make sure that we are the best one out of them, but it will be hopefully a good battle.”

It proved to be a difficult outing on the other side of the Red Bull garage for Isack Hadjar, who retired in the opening laps of the Sprint due to a mechanical issue.

“I didn’t really have power at the start,” the Frenchman summarised afterwards. “Then it sounded very bad and I had to retire the car, so very straightforward.”

title: McLaren drivers give verdicts on their Singapore Sprint collision
excerpt:
McLaren drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have given their perspectives on the collision between the pair during the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint.

The duo were circulating closely together in fourth and fifth during Saturday's Sprint on the streets around Marina Bay, which was also held in mixed conditions after a heavy downpour just before the start.

With the pair bottled up behind Charles Leclerc's Ferrari, as the Monegasque driver struggled with worn intermediate tyres, Norris made a move on Piastri on the final lap at Turn 5 in a bid for fourth place.

After diving to the inside and pulling alongside, Norris began to back out through the corner, with the reigning World Champion's left-front tyre catching the right-rear of Piastri's McLaren.

Both were sent into a spin, with Piastri hitting the wall and retiring while Norris was able to resume and reach the chequered flag in P8. Following a post-Sprint investigation the stewards opted for no further action to be taken.

"I think the pace was very strong. Obviously we were just stuck the whole race, and the last lap there was a big opportunity into Turn 5," said Norris on the incident.

"I went for it, the gap closed a bit more than I would have liked. Obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing, so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one.

"It was a big gap, I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri admitted that he struggled at the beginning and towards the end of the Sprint, with the Australian managing his worn intermediate tyres on an all-but dry track as he tried to pass Leclerc.

"I need to look at it. I didn't see him at the apex," said Piastri on the incident with Norris.

"I looked behind into the corner and saw he was a reasonable way behind for a corner like that but I'll have a look and the team can do what it needs to do."

title: Russell reacts to ‘silly’ crash in Singapore Sprint
excerpt:
George Russell has taken full responsibility for the crash that ended his Sprint in Singapore, admitting that it was the result of overconfidence and a “very silly mistake”.

On a weekend where the Mercedes driver will line up at the back of the grid for the Singapore Grand Prix, the Sprint represented his best chance of competing at the front of the field.

Starting from P2, Russell enjoyed a fantastic launch that saw him pass Max Verstappen for the lead, and he initially managed the tough conditions well after heavy rain made parts of the circuit harder to drive than others.

That was proved when the Briton came around the final corner and dipped his right rear wheel onto the painted white line, which sent him into a spin before he crashed into the pit wall. He was then flung back across the track and came to a halt, bringing an early end to his Sprint.

“I just misjudged it, to be honest,” he reflected. “I came round the corner, I came on the throttle, I got more power than I was expecting from the battery.

“I went a little bit wide and then I touched the white line. The number one rule in the rain is don’t touch the white line. It’s a very silly mistake – overly confident. I think it’s my first crash of the year. It’s annoying to happen from that position.”

While Russell wasn’t the only one caught out as a further eight drivers went on to retire from the event, including McLaren’s Oscar Piastri after he collided with his team mate Lando Norris, his incoming grid penalty for Sunday’s race made the error even more frustrating.

Nevertheless, Deputy Team Principal Bradley Lord was confident that Russell, who is running an older specification of the W17 to provide a direct comparison to Kimi Antonelli’s upgraded car, will be able to improve back to the points in the Grand Prix.

“There’s never been a Qualifying session we less need him to compete in, so if [the car] can’t be fixed, that’s okay because we know where he’s starting tomorrow regardless,” Lord explained. “We’ll try and get him out. We think it should [involve] swapping the rear end, right front corner and hopefully the floor isn’t too badly damaged. It didn’t look it, but you never know.

“It’s hopefully not the only opportunity to get a couple of points – there’s still some on offer tomorrow. Super disappointed obviously. He had a great start, great first lap, pulled a second on Max and then unfortunately had a bit of a power surge as he came through the last corner.

“You get the clipped power at full throttle, you get more power until you get to full throttle, and I think that surged. Then the right rear went on the kerb and it spun up. We saw what happened after that.”

Contrastingly, Antonelli improved from his start position of P7 to finish P4 at the chequered flag, capitalising on the misfortune of some drivers ahead whilst Mercedes continued to learn more about the upgrade package they introduced in Malaysia.

Asked whether the car felt better in the Sprint, the Italian replied: “Yeah, I mean we tried some things and it did feel a little bit better. We will make some changes going into Qualifying and hopefully they will help us a little bit because the window seems very small where this package operates.

“We saw some good things last night and hopefully we can improve some things and extract the potential out of the package. I truly believe that there is potential in this package. We just need to find the right balance and hopefully we can improve our pace.”

title: Verstappen wins Sprint as Russell crashes and McLarens collide
excerpt:
Max Verstappen followed up his victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia by winning Saturday’s Sprint around the streets of Singapore – mastering the mixed weather conditions while George Russell crashed out early on and the McLaren drivers clashed in the closing stages.

After a pre-race downpour, which soaked the first and third sectors of the Marina Bay Street Circuit, while leaving the middle sector merely damp, the action got under way around half an hour later than planned, with all drivers running the intermediate tyres.

In a repeat of last weekend’s start at Sepang, Russell charged past polesitter Verstappen in the slippery conditions and initially drove into the distance, only to undo that work by dramatically crashing at the final corner of the first lap.

Verstappen moved back into the lead as a result and, after nailing the race restart, the Dutchman never looked back – managing his intermediate tyres in ever-drying conditions and steadily pulling away from the Ferraris and McLarens behind.

Lewis Hamilton led the Ferrari charge after a rapid getaway that turned sixth into third (which became second when Russell crashed), over Charles Leclerc and McLaren team mates Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, who engaged in battle during the final laps.

With Leclerc reporting that his intermediate tyres were heavily worn on the drying track, and the McLaren cars closing in, Norris tagged Piastri as their lines converged at Turn 5, sent both into a spin, and flipped the situation on its head.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli took advantage to cross the line in fourth, with Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson, Haas’ Ollie Bearman and Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg also benefitting, as Norris slipped to eighth and Piastri stopped outright.

Pierre Gasly (Alpine), Esteban Ocon (Haas), Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin), Carlos Sainz (Williams) and Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) were the last drivers to reach the chequered flag in an attritional race, while Piastri classified in a lapped 14th.

Alex Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas failed to finish in their Williams, Audi and Cadillac machines after a three-car collision; Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto both stopped in the early laps; while Cadillac’s Sergio Perez and Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll collided on the first tour.

AS IT HAPPENED

At the end of an exciting Sprint Qualifying session around the Marina Bay venue, it was Verstappen who grabbed pole from Russell, Leclerc and Piastri – the Dutchman subsequently avoiding a grid penalty after being investigated for a yellow flag incident in SQ1.

There was one change to the Sprint grid in the build-up to lights out, though, with Sainz – due to start at the very back of the field – moving to the pit lane when Williams carried out suspension set-up changes on his car under Parc Ferme Conditions.

As drivers got ready for the first ever Sprint in Singapore, they did so under extremely overcast skies and a growing threat of rain. Would it come down and cause some drama? Or would it break up around the circuit amid the intense heat?

Around 10 minutes away from the scheduled 1700 start, the answer came in the form of a downpour that soaked parts of the track – gazebos going up on the grid to cover the F1 cars, and the Medical Car being sent out to assess the conditions.

Following that track inspection, where the Medical Car splashed its way through plenty of puddles, the FIA confirmed that the start would be delayed – standing water at Turn 2 and 3 noted as particularly troublesome at this stage.

While the Medical Car carried out its latest inspections, the Mercedes drivers provided some light entertainment – Russell, having returned to the garage, surprising Antonelli with a message over the radio. “Who is this? Oh, George!” Antonelli chuckled, still sitting in his car on the grid.

At 1717, Race Control confirmed a 1730 formation lap, prompting drivers who had been sheltering in the pit lane to join those – like the aforementioned Antonelli – who had remained tucked into their cockpits under the gazebos.

As the clock hit half past, the Safety Car duly led the field away – the FIA adding that they anticipated at least two formation laps. All drivers were on the intermediate tyres, with some parts of the track still much wetter than others.

“The spray is very bad,” reported Piastri, fourth in the queue, as he navigated the first sector of the lap. The middle sector appeared to be much better – almost “completely dry” according to Lawson – before conditions worsened again through the last few corners.

After a couple of formation laps, Race Control settled on a standing start. “There’s a good chance we’ll go to slicks at some point,” reported Albon as the cars gradually lined up on the grid, and anticipation built for what could be a wild encounter.

When the lights went out, Russell made a clean getaway to pass Verstappen into Turn 1, with Hamilton vaulting to third over Leclerc, Piastri and Norris. Despite the tricky, slippery conditions, there were no major dramas to report in the opening corners.

However, disaster struck for leader Russell at the very end of the first lap when he lost control of his car exiting the final corner, slid across the track and slammed into the concrete wall. “I’m fine. Sorry, sorry, sorry,” the Briton lamented over the radio afterwards.

Russell was not the only early retirement, with Perez and Stroll coming to blows under braking for Turn 16 – the Aston Martin out on the spot, and the Cadillac limping back to the pits (the stewards ultimately opting against handing out any penalties). Hadjar (coming to a halt at Turn 5) and Colapinto (stopping at Turn 14) then made it five DNFs in as many laps.

“It’s drying very quickly,” Piastri reported on the radio, as drivers maintained position behind the Safety Car. Everyone bar Lindblad, that was – replays showing him spinning out and dropping to last place, which was now 17th after those retirements.

At the end of Lap 6, the Safety Car lights switched off and racing resumed, with Verstappen keeping the lead over Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli. Behind, Bearman pulled a smart move on Gasly through Turns 1/2/3 for P8 and the final points-paying position.

Bortoleto, Albon and Bottas all pitted following an unseen incident at the restart. Replays then showed the Williams going into the back of the Audi, and the Cadillac going into the back of the Williams. Bortoleto and Bottas both retired, while Albon pressed on. Meanwhile, the stewards noted Hamilton for a potential yellow flag breach.

Live cameras then cut to Hulkenberg clearing Gasly for ninth position into Turn 1. “He pushed me wide. Hulkenberg didn’t leave me space,” the Alpine driver argued over the radio, to no avail, before losing another spot to the Haas of Ocon.

Halfway through proceedings, Verstappen led Hamilton by 1.3 seconds – the latter commenting that track was edging closer and closer to dry conditions, but still too wet in places. Leclerc sat third, from Piastri, Norris and Antonelli, with Lawson and Bearman rounding out the top eight.

While the track continued to dry out over the next few laps, nobody felt the need to pit for slick tyres. “We’re thinking ahead to a Safety Car. How far away is it from dry [tyres]?”, Norris was asked by his engineer. “It’s not,” came his response.

Around the same time, Leclerc reported that his front tyres were now “destroyed”, bringing increased pressure from Piastri and Norris behind. McLaren’s hopes of snatching a podium were dashed, though, when Norris launched a move on Piastri into Turn 5 and the pair made contact.

That incident meant Leclerc followed Verstappen and Hamilton home in third, while Antonelli climbed to fourth over Lawson, Bearman and Hulkenberg, and Norris was left to ponder what might have been in eighth. The stewards later reviewed the coming together but did not issue a penalty.

Gasly took ninth after his early bid for points faded, followed by Ocon, Alonso, Sainz and Lindblad. All of them cleared Piastri, who ended up in the wall and in a lapped 14th – the Australian having lost a whopping 10 places as a result of that intra-team collision.

Albon was a late retirement following his contact with Bortoleto and Bottas, with the stewards set to look into the moment the Williams rear-ended the Audi post-race. A separate note from the panel confirmed that there would be no further action over Hamilton’s alleged yellow flag incident.

Hadjar, Colapinto, Russell, Perez and Stroll watched most of the Sprint from the sidelines after their respective early-race dramas – the Mercedes man losing another five points to team mate Antonelli in the Drivers’ Championship standings, and now sitting 89 back.

Key quote

“I mean, the start was horrendous again, so that’s definitely something that we need to improve on, because if you have something like that tomorrow, that’s your race over, if nothing crazy happens,” said winner Verstappen. “So, yeah, not ideal, but then we got a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner. And after that, we just wanted to keep it calm and under control, because you know that you can’t pass around here, and especially in a condition like this with the intermediates. So, we just tried to bring it home, and of course, I’m happy to win here in the Sprint, but I also know that I want to win tomorrow, not today.”

What’s next

Following the Sprint, the drivers will be back on track during Qualifying for the Singapore Grand Prix later on Saturday at 2100 local time. Head to the RACE HUB to find out how you can follow the action.

title: Why Wolff is backing Mercedes’ split-spec strategy
excerpt:
Toto Wolff believes that the decision to split the car specifications between Kimi Antonelli and George Russell in Singapore is a necessary “compromise” to work out why the upgraded Mercedes seems “a little more tricky to drive”.

Instead of bringing regular tweaks to their challenger, the Silver Arrows waited until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to introduce their first major update in four months – which failed to deliver the boost that they had predicted.

For that reason, they chose to revert Russell to the specification they last ran in Azerbaijan – where he dominated Qualifying and won the Grand Prix – and directly compare him to his team mate.

Contrastingly, Antonelli was to remain in the upgraded W17 and test a new front wing in order to gather some conclusive data, but nevertheless ended up finishing behind the Briton in both FP1 and Sprint Qualifying.

After admitting that the Marina Bay Street Circuit is an outlier on the calendar, Team Principal Wolff explained: “There is a pattern, but most importantly is to really dissect what's working and what's not on the old and the new spec and then finding a way forward, picking the best bits and seeing where the development direction needs to get us in order to extract the optimum lap time.

“Now, having said that, obviously running two different cars is not always ideal, but it's a compromise we just need to take. So, we have two test pilots at the moment. We need to take it in order to ensure that we're doing the right thing for next year as well.

“The new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it.

“The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point. It will be needing more time to really come to more conclusive information. We've put a few months of upgrades into the car, clearly pointing in a direction that we think is advantageous, and maybe we just need to calibrate it a little bit in order to find the right way forward for 2027.”

Although Mercedes dominated the early rounds of 2026 – which helped them build the 151-point advantage they currently hold over Ferrari in the Teams’ Championship – their frontrunning rivals have gradually closed the gap, with the Scuderia, McLaren and Red Bull all claiming race wins.

The upgrade was intended to regain some of that lost performance, but Wolff conceded that putting their resources into one big package could be considered a risky decision.

“I think that we are one of those large organisations that needs to be very careful how and when we spend our cost cap money,” he said. “We felt that the right strategic decision was to work towards a bigger one and then introduce it.

“Obviously, with the risk of if it doesn't work as you've anticipated, it's just quite difficult to dial yourself out and understand why it hasn't worked. So, it's something which we will look at in the future. Maybe we'll do smaller steps, and then if there is a warning light, it's easier to undo.”

His drivers had their own thoughts on Mercedes' latest strategy after Russell clinched P2 in Sprint Qualifying while Antonelli looked to be significantly off the pace, finishing six-tenths down on his team mate in P7.

Understandably encouraged by his performance, Russell said: “I can definitely confirm the old one is not bad. Let’s see what tomorrow brings with Kimi on the upgrade.

“As a team, there’s still nothing telling us that it isn’t working, but it’s a sport driven by the stopwatch, and the stopwatch has not been great for the upgrade yet. Let’s see, and maybe tomorrow’s a different day.”

“I think it's going to be a difficult weekend, unless we can pull something out tomorrow,” added Antonelli. “It's going to be very tricky. I don't really see where we can find seven-tenths [to Max Verstappen], but you never know.

“Maybe tonight, Bono [Peter Bonnington], the engineers, we're going to find something in the car. And for sure, I'm going to try to improve a little bit the driving, and then we'll see tomorrow where we end up.”

title: Three F1 drivers learn stewards decision into chain-reaction accident
excerpt:
F1 stewards have elected to take no further action against Gabriel Bortoleto, Alex Albon, or Valtteri Bottas for an incident which ultimately saw all three eliminated from the Singapore Sprint.

The Audi, Williams, and Cadillac drivers all retired from the sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit after a chain-reaction accident at the end of lap six, just as the field was preparing to go green-flag racing after the early safety car was withdrawn.

Bortoleto, at the head of the trio, checked up behind the Aston Martin of Fernando Alonso as the field began to pace themselves, with this happening at Turn 16 - the left-hander of the final chicane.

But in doing so, Albon rammed into the back of the Audi, with Bottas then in turn doing the same to Albon, with all three cars immediately pitting, with Bortoleto and Bottas retiring on the spot, whilst Albon staggered on before eventually being called into retirement himself.

All three drivers were summoned by the stewards to answer for the incident, with the panel ultimately deciding that no penalties would be applied.

A stewards document read: "When preparing for the re-start at the end of a safety car period, car 23 [Albon] collided with the rear of car 5 [Bortoleto], and car 77 [Bottas] collided with the rear of car 23.

"The driver of car 23 said that he had no opportunity to avoid colliding with the rear of car 5 after car 5 braked hard to avoid a collision with the cars in front.

"In the stewards’ assessment both collisions were a consequence of a concertina created by cars ahead travelling at inconsistent speeds in the preparation for the restart.

"As cars 23 and 77 were towards the back of the pack of slow moving cars, the chain reaction effect on them was more pronounced.

"Nonetheless, the stewards determined that like the collision between cars 77 and 23, the collision between cars 23 and 5 could have been avoided had the driver of car 23 recognised the risk of a concertina ahead and left more space when following car 5, particularly having regard to the damp conditions.

"Had car 23 not retired from the Sprint as a consequence of the collision, the stewards would have imposed a 5 second time penalty rather than the usual 10 second time penalty taking into account that, in part at least, a number of cars ahead in the queue had contributed by slowing at inconsistent rates.

"A 5 second time penalty would not have been converted into a grid penalty and therefore the stewards determined not to apply a penalty in this case."

title: Isack Hadjar Singapore GP misery continues despite power unit change
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar's wretched day in Singapore continued after failing to set a time in qualifying for Sunday's grand prix.

In the sprint race earlier in the day, Hadjar was forced to pull his RB22 off the circuit due to a power unit problem as the field toured behind the safety car following a crash at the end of lap one involving George Russell in his Mercedes.

During the interval between the sprint and qualifying at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, the Red Bull mechanics replaced the PU, allowing Hadjar to start qualifying. The French-Algerian driver even thanked the team as he returned to the track.

It was not long, however, before he encountered further issues. Initially, he was forced to stop on track, but managed to get the car going again and return to the garage.

Despite another attempt to post a lap, Hadjar then complained of a gearbox problem. "Same issue, I've lost the gears!" bemoaned Hadjar. The team then retired the car from qualifying.

Explaining the situation to Sky Sports F1, team principal Laurent Mekies said: "Nothing Isack could have done differently, but we had a gearbox issue on his car.

"Obviously, it comes after the issue we had with the power unit in the sprint and the incredible push from everyone to turn on the car and replace everything that had to be replaced.

"A bit early to understand the exact cause. It appears to be a gearbox issue, but we will conduct the right analysis."

title: Lando Norris discovers stewards verdict into nightmare Oscar Piastri crash
excerpt:
Lando Norris has escaped punishment from the Singapore Grand Prix stewards following his collision with McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri in the sprint race.

On the final lap of the Sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, with Piastri running ahead in fourth, Norris attempted to pass the sister car at Turn 5 with a lunge to the inside, only for his left-front tyre to tag Piastri's right-rear, sending both cars spinning off.

Piastri hit the barrier and retired on the spot whilst Norris was able to get going again and finished in eighth place, picking up a single point, albeit with the incident costing McLaren eight points, having been on for a haul of nine with a four-five finish.

The incident was sent to the stewards, with Norris allegedly causing a collision, only to avoid a penalty.

A stewards' report read: "The driver of car 1 [Norris] attempted to overtake car 81 [Piastri] on the inside at Turn 5. A collision occurred at the apex.

"The driver of car 81 explained that he had not expected car 1 to attempt an overtake and, after turning in, noticed car 1 on the inside and attempted to leave space.

"The driver of car 1 said that he saw an opportunity to overtake. He said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of car 81 prior to the apex and therefore expected to be left space.

"As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated, so he had to use the inside kerb and braked, and a collision occurred.

"The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision.

"Therefore, the stewards determined to take no further action

title: Haas reveal brutal reason behind Esteban Ocon axe
excerpt:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has outlined why the American squad felt it "needed" to drop Esteban Ocon.

Ocon will not have his contract with the Kannapolis-based outfit and will leave at the end of the current F1 season.

The Frenchman does not have any confirmed plans for next year, but is determined to stay in the F1 paddock and is not entertaining racing in a different championship, even if that means a campaign on the sidelines.

Haas is yet to announce Ocon's replacement, but the choice is understood to have been trimmed down to a straight fight between Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, who leads the F2 championship, and Haas reserve and former Alpine driver Jack Doohan.

Oliver Bearman is expected to continue on the other side of the Haas garage, although that has not been formally announced at this stage.

Asked what the decision to let Ocon go came down to, Komatsu told Sky Sports F1: "When we're choosing a driver, it's about the overall performance of our package, and then everything comes into it.

"Of course, natural talent — that's something we cannot teach. As a driver, you are either quick or not quick.

"Esteban is very, very quick on his day. When the car is perfect, when he's happy with the car, he's very, very quick.

"But what we're looking for going forward is we just want the speed plus more consistency, and then also the feedback as well."

Komatsu: Ocon needs an environment he can 'flourish' in

Komatsu moved to defend Ocon, highlighting how strong he is when the car is in the right window and the conditions suit him.

However, he also pointed out that the one-time grand prix winner may thrive in a more established setting than the American team can offer.

"Esteban is very good; I don't want to take anything away from him," the Haas boss added. "What he's done, he contributed a lot to the team, and he's still the very fast race winner we signed, right?

"As a team, we are still on the journey, so we still have a lot of imperfections. Maybe in a better environment, a perfect environment, Esteban can completely flourish his talent.

"But with the team set up as we are, with some inconsistencies, issues, etc., it's really not playing to Esteban's strengths sometimes. So we needed to make some changes."

title: F1 makes sprint history in dramatic eight-car retirement madness
excerpt:
The Singapore Sprint was one for the ages!

The Singapore Grand Prix Sprint has become the most chaotic in F1's short sprint history, with nine drivers failing to reach the chequered flag at Marina Bay on Saturday.

Max Verstappen crossed the line first after 20 laps around the street circuit, with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc completing the podium.

But the race behind them was defined by a string of retirements that eclipsed anything seen since sprint races were introduced in 2021.

George Russell was the first of the nine to fall by the wayside after crashing at the end of the first lap, before Cadillac's Sergio Perez ran into Lance Stroll in his Aston Martin to send them both into retirement. Franco Colapinto suffered an ERS failure soon after in his Alpine.

As the safety car ended, at the conclusion of lap six, Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas ran into the back of Alex Albon in his Williams, who in turn hit the Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto. Bottas and Bortoleto returned to their garages and retired; Albon did so later in the race.

Oscar Piastri also failed to finish, taking the total to nine, after he was taken out by McLaren team-mate Lando Norris on the final lap. However, he was a classified finisher in 14th. It means eight drivers were classified as retirements.

The sheer spread of teams affected, from Red Bull and Mercedes to Williams, Audi, Cadillac, Aston Martin and Alpine, underlined how widespread the carnage was through the Singapore streets.

The previous record for most Sprint DNFs

Until Saturday, the record for the most retirements in a sprint had stood since the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix, where five drivers failed to finish.

That sprint at Lusail began unravelling almost immediately, with Liam Lawson spinning into the gravel at Turn 2 on the opening lap.

Logan Sargeant added to the carnage three laps later, beaching his Williams at Turn 9 and triggering a second safety car.

The most dramatic moment came on lap 11, when Perez, Esteban Ocon and Nico Hulkenberg collided three-wide into Turn 2 while fighting for position.

Perez and Ocon were stranded immediately, while Hulkenberg limped back to the pits before retiring. Stewards later classed the incident as a racing accident, with no driver found predominantly at fault.

Singapore has now surpassed that mark by three retirements, cementing Saturday's sprint as the most attrition-hit in the format's history.

Five drivers also retired from the 2025 United States Grand Prix sprint, although failed to surpass the the feat seen in Qatar.

title: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri tight-lipped after latest McLaren collision
excerpt:
Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri kept their cards close to their chests following another damaging collision between the McLaren duo.

On the last lap of a rain-affected Singapore Sprint race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, Norris opted to dive down the inside of Piastri at the Turn 5 right-hander as he pushed for fourth place.

Clearly blind-sided, Piastri did not see Norris to his right and on the inside, leading to the duo crashing into one another. Whilst Norris was able to continue to finish eighth, Piastri retired immediately.

Addressing the collision on Sky Sports F1, Norris was reticent with his answers. "I’d rather just go back and review it," was his initial response when asked, before stating, from his perspective, that the move on Piastri "was" on.

As to whether the team had said anything to him yet, he replied: “I apologised to them that one of the cars is out but, as I said, the rest of it we’ll go review.”

From his cockpit point of view, Piastri remarked: "It’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I’m not that bothered either way.

"Just obviously it’s a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed. Just a shame for the team.”

title: When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' world championship?
excerpt:
When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' championship title?

Following the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix Sprint, Kimi Antonelli holds an 89-point lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

No other driver is within 100 points of the Italian, who is increasingly set to become the youngest F1 world champion and shatter Sebastian Vettel's record of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by over three years.

Antonelli, who turned 20 in August 2026, has dominated the season, but when can the Mercedes driver become the first Italian to be crowned world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953?

The article continues below.

THIS ARTICLE WILL BE UPDATED FOLLOWING EVERY GRAND PRIX UNTIL ANTONELLI WINS THE 2026 F1 WORLD DRIVERS' TITLE.

When can Kimi Antonelli win the title?

After the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint, there are seven races scheduled to take place in the season, each worth 25 points.

This gives a total of 175 points remaining in the championship, with Antonelli holding that 89-point lead after fourth in the Singapore Sprint whilst Russell crashed out from the lead in the wet conditions.

A scenario exists whereby Antonelli could win the title in the United States, which is laid out below.

Antonelli wins in Singapore; Russell scores 0 points. The gap extends to 114 points.

Following Singapore, 150 points will remain in the season, with Antonelli potentially holding a 114-point lead, with 125 remaining following the trip to Austin.

It would mean that heading to the United States GP in Austin, Russell would be required to win every grand prix, with Antonelli only requiring to score 11 points, meaning he could win the title with a fourth-place finish in Austin

If Antonelli is exactly 125 points ahead of Russell after the Austin race, he would win the title on wins countback, as he would hold nine victories to Russell on three, which could climb to eight over the final five races.

title: F1 qualifying delay confirmed after torrential downpour triggers Singapore Sprint chaos
excerpt:
Qualifying for the Singapore Grand Prix has been pushed back by 30 minutes after a chaotic, rain-hit Sprint race at Marina Bay, with the session now set to begin at 21:30 local time.

The disruption began before a wheel had even turned. Torrential rain swept across the street circuit shortly before the sprint was due to start, forcing officials to delay the race itself by 30 minutes as standing water made conditions too dangerous for a start.

Once underway, the sprint quickly descended into chaos. George Russell crashed out in his Mercedes, bringing out the safety car and further disrupting the running order on the tight, barrier-lined layout.

By the finish, eight drivers had failed to see the chequered flag, with Oscar Piastri, Alexander Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto, Valtteri Bottas, Isack Hadjar, Russell, Sergio Pérez and Lance Stroll all retiring.

Max Verstappen emerged victorious ahead of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, with Kimi Antonelli completing the top four.

Why qualifying must be delayed

The knock-on effect on qualifying stems directly from FIA sporting regulations governing sprint weekends, which require at least three hours between the chequered flag in the sprint and the start of qualifying.

With the sprint finishing later than scheduled, that mandatory gap pushed qualifying back by the same 30 minutes.

The delay also affects the setup window for teams. Parc ferme conditions, which restrict changes to car specification, lift once the sprint ends and remain open until cars leave the pit lane for qualifying.

That window has shifted later alongside the new start time, giving teams until 21:30 to finalise any adjustments before parc ferme regulations are reinstated for the rest of the event.

title: Max Verstappen demands Red Bull fix after latest 'horrendous' situation
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has called on Red Bull to correct the "horrendous" starts he continues to encounter following his sprint victory ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix.

Starts have continually been an issue for Red Bull this season, underlined last weekend in wet conditions at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and again on a wet track for the start of the sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

In Malaysia, polesitter Verstappen was swallowed up by Mercedes duo George Russell and Kimi Antonelli; in Singapore, again from pole, the four-time F1 champion was passed on the short run-down to Turn 1 by Russell.

The Briton then crashed out of the sprint at the end of the opening lap, handing the lead, and eventually the win, to Verstappen.

Reflecting on his race, Verstappen said: "The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something we need to improve on because if that happens tomorrow, that's the race over, if nothing crazy happens, so not ideal.

"We then got a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner, and after that, you just want to keep it calm and under control because you know you can't pass around here, especially in conditions like this with the intermediates.

"So I just tried to bring it home. I'm quite happy to win here in the sprint, but I want to win tomorrow, not today."

Verstappen has now won on every grand prix circuit on which he has competed, but he naturally dismissed his sprint win.

"I want to win tomorrow," he said. "I don't see this as a win, in terms of winning a grand prix, so we need to have a good qualifying.

"It will be very close with a lot of cars, so we need to make sure we are the best one out of them, but hopefully a good battle."

title: McLaren last-lap horror as Lando Norris takes out Oscar Piastri
excerpt:
McLaren suffered a horrific final lap of the Singapore Sprint, as Lando Norris took out Oscar Piastri.

Piastri and Norris had been running in fourth and fifth for the entirety of the sprint at the Marina Bay Circuit from the end of the first lap onwards, following a crash for George Russell.

The sprint took place in wet conditions following a torrential downpour ahead of the 100 km race, which was delayed by 30 minutes due to the weather.

Both McLarens closed rapidly on Charles Leclerc in the closing laps, before Norris attempted an overtake on Piastri at Turn 5.

While there was space, the gap rapidly closed, with Norris hitting his team-mate who was unable to finish the race as a result.

Norris recovered from both McLarens spinning to finish in eighth, while Piastri had to walk back to the paddock.

The reigning world champion did apologise on the radio, saying: "Yeah, sorry about that. Obviously, I didn't want that to happen, but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex."

Norris is under investigation for causing a collision.

title: Max Verstappen takes advantage of George Russell crash as F1 sets new sprint record
excerpt:
Max Verstappen took full advantage of an opening-lap crash from George Russell to clinch victory in the Singapre Grand Prix sprint.

The 20-lap race was delayed for 30 minutes after a torrential downpour struck the Marina Bay Street Circuit 15 minutes before the scheduled start time.

Following two formation laps behind the safety car, and with no technical glitches on this occasion, unlike ahead of the Bahrain GP in Malaysia last weekend when chaos struck, racing finally got underway.

From second position on the grid, Russell made a superb start to get ahead of Verstappen on the short run-down to Turn 1, whilst Lewis Hamilton rose three places from sixth to third in his Ferrari.

But at the end of the opening lap, Russell made an error coming out of the final corner, catching a wet kerb that sent him into a spin into a wall along the start-finish straight, handing the lead to Verstappen and sparking an obvious safety car.

Once that disappeared at the end of lap six, the race turned into a procession, with Verstappen going on to clinch his 14th win from the 30 sprints there have been overall in F1, followed by Hamilton and Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

[Article continues below]

Record set for an F1 sprint

Behind the safety car on the formation laps, it was clear that whilst the majority of the circuit was wet, there were other sections "completely dry", such as Turn 13, as reported by Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, and it became a question of when the drivers would pit for slicks, if at all.

Russell's crash quickly became the major talking point once racing got underway. With his W17 stranded on the straight, it led to the remaining drivers filing through the pit lane, with Lance Stroll in his Aston Martin and the Cadillac of Sergio Perez also retiring soon after following a collision between the duo.

They were remarkably joined by the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar, who pulled off into an escape road at Turn 5 due to a lack of engine braking.

Soon after, as the safety car continued, Franco Colapinto joined the list of retirees due to his Alpine shutting down. It left 17 cars in the race once the safety car departed at the end of lap six.

But that number was swiftly reduced to 15 as Williams' Alex Albon went into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto in his Audi, whilst the second Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas joined the concertina by running into Albon.

Although Albon returned to the pits for a new front wing and rejoined the race, Audi and Cadillac opted to retire Bortoleto and Bottas, taking the number to seven, a record for a sprint. That later became eight when Albon was asked by Williams to pit and retire the car.

The stewards later confirmed they would be investigating the Perez-Stroll and Albon-Bortoleto incidents after the race.

On the final lap, there was drama as Lando Norris tried to overtake McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri for fourth place, only for them to collide. Whilst Norris was able to continue and finish eighth, Piastri became the ninth retiree.

Behind the podium trio, the points-paying positions were completed by Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, Lawson, Oliver Bearman in his Haas, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, and then Norris.

With Antonelli collecting an additional five points, he has now opened up a gap of 89 points over Russell, who will start the GP at the back of the grid due to taking on a completely new power unit.

title: George Russell suffers scary crash in delayed Singapore Sprint

title: Torrential rain again sparks chaos and jeopardy as Singapore GP sprint delayed
excerpt:
Just six days after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was heavily disrupted by a torrential downpour, the weather struck again over the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Just 15 minutes before the start of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint, the F1 first race of its kind in the island state, rain started to fall and very quickly became torrential.

The 11 teams, who had been preparing the cars on the grid, were again forced to scramble, erecting awnings to keep the machinery, mechanics and drivers dry.

Eight minutes later, the FIA confirmed there would be a delayed start due to the rain, pointing out there to be "a large amount of standing water around turns 2 and 3".

Although the rain eased, it continued to fall steadily. A second tour of the track from the medical car highlighted that issues given the standing water in certain places.

Another inspection lap was confirmed for quarter past the hour, after which the medical car reported conditions had improved, and there would be a formation lap at half past the hour.

The FIA confirmed there would be two formation laps behind the safety car. The drivers were then informed there would be a standing start.

title: Pit lane start confirmed for Singapore Sprint after late change made
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz will start the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint from the pit lane after Williams changed the suspension set-up on his car under parc ferme conditions.

The Spaniard qualified last for the Sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, finishing P22 in a difficult Sprint qualifying session that saw both Williams drivers eliminated in SQ1.

Sainz endured a troubled session, having already experienced brake problems during Friday’s sole practice session. The 31-year-old explained that the team had made changes to address those issues, but admitted they were not ideal.

He also locked up at Turn 8 during his flying lap, further compromising his effort, while a loss of power left him frustrated with the final outcome.

Team-mate Alex Albon fared marginally better, qualifying P19 with a time of 1:36.130, while Sainz recorded a 1:37.376.

The pit lane start means Sainz will have a difficult task making progress in the 21-lap Sprint, although the additional running could provide Williams with useful information ahead of Saturday evening’s grand prix qualifying.

Sainz’s qualifying difficulties were compounded by an issue with Overtake Mode following the red flag in SQ1.

The session was interrupted after Sergio Perez crashed his Cadillac at Turn 5, with debris left on the circuit after the Mexican driver continued towards the pits.

The FIA subsequently acknowledged that a human error in race control meant Overtake Mode was not available immediately after the restart. The system was then activated for just 27 seconds before being disabled again, affecting cars depending on their position on track.

Sainz claimed the power disparity had cost him around half a second, with several other drivers also potentially disadvantaged. The FIA confirmed the incident was separate from a timing-system issue that had also disrupted the session.

Williams will now hope to make the most of the Sprint before the team turns its attention to grand prix qualifying.
